CH01_SC01_002_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH01_SC01_002_NARRATOR.caption: At one preparation station, two finalists are approaching the most important moment of their competition. Mariam Al Mansoori and Saeed Al Nuaimi are close to completing their dessert. But time is running out. Only twelve minutes remain before the final judging round.

CH01_SC02_001_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH01_SC02_001_MARIAM.caption: Saeed, we are almost finished. I need the sugar and the baking soda for the final stage.

CH01_SC02_002_SAEED.speaker: SAEED
CH01_SC02_002_SAEED.caption: I’ll get them now. The judges could arrive at any moment.

CH01_SC03_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH01_SC03_001_NARRATOR.caption: On the preparation counter are three sealed containers. Each container holds a fine white powder. Their identification labels are attached, and the ingredients appear to be ready for use.

CH01_SC04_002_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH01_SC04_002_NARRATOR.caption: One falls. Then another. Then the third.

CH01_SC04_005_SAEED.speaker: SAEED
CH01_SC04_005_SAEED.caption: I can’t tell which container is which.

CH01_SC05_001_SAEED.speaker: SAEED
CH01_SC05_001_SAEED.caption: They all look almost exactly the same. One should be sugar, one should be baking soda, and one should be salt, but the labels are no longer connected to the containers.

CH01_SC05_002_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH01_SC05_002_MARIAM.caption: We cannot guess. Using the wrong ingredient could ruin the recipe.

CH01_SC06_001_FATIMA.speaker: FATIMA
CH01_SC06_001_FATIMA.caption: Stop preparation immediately. Do not open or use any of those containers.

CH01_SC06_002_SAEED.speaker: SAEED
CH01_SC06_002_SAEED.caption: Even if we think we know which one is the sugar?

CH01_SC06_003_FATIMA.speaker: FATIMA
CH01_SC06_003_FATIMA.caption: Thinking is not enough. The ingredients are no longer reliably identified. Until we have defensible evidence and a safe course of action, they must remain isolated.

CH01_SC07_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH01_SC07_001_NARRATOR.caption: Hamad Al Zaabi, a field investigator in applied chemistry, arrives at the station carrying a tablet and a compact evidence kit.

CH01_SC07_005_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH01_SC07_005_HAMAD.caption: I need your help. From this point forward, you are our junior food chemistry investigator. Your task is to examine the evidence, identify what the tests can and cannot prove, and recommend the safest final action.

CH01_SC07_006_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH01_SC07_006_HAMAD.caption: Do not rely on appearance. Do not rely on assumptions. Follow the evidence.

CH02_DEC01_001_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_DEC01_001_HAMAD.caption: Three powders may look identical while behaving very differently at the molecular level. We need a test that produces measurable and comparable evidence. What should we do first?

CH02_DEC01_APPEARANCE_1_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH02_DEC01_APPEARANCE_1_MARIAM.caption: They are all white. Any slight visual difference could come from lighting, particle size, or the container itself.

CH02_DEC01_APPEARANCE_2_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_DEC01_APPEARANCE_2_HAMAD.caption: Correct. Color alone cannot establish chemical identity. Choose a method that produces measurable evidence.

CH02_DEC01_CORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_DEC01_CORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Good choice. Conductivity can help us determine whether dissolved particles are able to carry electrical charge. We will test each sample separately under identical conditions.

CH02_DEC01_MIX_1_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_DEC01_MIX_1_HAMAD.caption: Mixing them would destroy the separation between the samples and reduce the value of the evidence. It could also create an unnecessary reaction or contamination risk.

CH02_DEC01_TASTE_1_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_DEC01_TASTE_1_HAMAD.caption: Stop. We never taste an unidentified substance. A familiar appearance does not prove that a substance is safe, food-grade, or uncontaminated.

CH02_SC11_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH02_SC11_001_NARRATOR.caption: The competition station becomes a temporary scientific investigation workspace. The three samples stay separated. Clean beakers, water, measuring tools, a conductivity probe, and a pH probe are prepared.

CH02_SC11_002_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC11_002_HAMAD.caption: To compare the samples fairly, every preparation condition must be the same. In this simulation, each solution is prepared using zero point one zero grams of material per one hundred millilitres of water, at twenty-five degrees Celsius.

CH02_SC12_001_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC12_001_HAMAD.caption: Before testing the samples, we need a control measurement.

CH02_SC12_003_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC12_003_HAMAD.caption: Correct. The water-only control tells us the background conductivity of the system before any sample is added.

CH02_SC12_005_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC12_005_SYSTEM.caption: Water-only control: two microsiemens per centimetre.

CH02_SC13_001_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC13_001_HAMAD.caption: Select Sample A and begin the first conductivity measurement.

CH02_SC13_003_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC13_003_SYSTEM.caption: Sample A conductivity: four microsiemens per centimetre.

CH02_SC13_005_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC13_005_HAMAD.caption: Correct. Sample A produces very few mobile charged particles under these simulation conditions.

CH02_SC13_006_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC13_006_HAMAD.caption: Record the observation, but do not identify the sample yet. One measurement is evidence, not a complete conclusion.

CH02_SC14_002_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC14_002_SYSTEM.caption: Sample B conductivity: one thousand one hundred microsiemens per centimetre.

CH02_SC14_003_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC14_003_SYSTEM.caption: Sample C conductivity: one thousand nine hundred and thirty microsiemens per centimetre.

CH02_SC14_006_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH02_SC14_006_MARIAM.caption: Does that prove Sample A is sugar?

CH02_SC14_007_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC14_007_HAMAD.caption: It supports that possibility within our candidate set. But conductivity alone does not provide a unique chemical identity.

CH02_SC15_001_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC15_001_HAMAD.caption: To understand the readings, we need to examine what happens at the atomic level.

CH02_SC15_003_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC15_003_HAMAD.caption: A neutral sodium atom has eleven protons and eleven electrons. When sodium loses one electron, it has one more proton than electrons. It becomes a positively charged sodium ion.

CH02_SC15_005_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC15_005_HAMAD.caption: Chlorine behaves differently. A neutral chlorine atom has seventeen protons and seventeen electrons. When chlorine gains an electron, it has one more electron than protons. It becomes a negatively charged chloride ion.

CH02_SC15_007_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC15_007_HAMAD.caption: Opposite charges attract. This electrostatic attraction forms an ionic bond.

CH02_SC15_008_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH02_SC15_008_NARRATOR.caption: When sodium chloride dissolves in water, sodium and chloride ions separate and move through the solution. Because the ions can carry charge, the solution conducts electricity.

CH02_SC15_009_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC15_009_HAMAD.caption: Sucrose also dissolves in water, but it remains mainly as electrically neutral molecules. Dissolving does not automatically mean forming ions.

CH02_SC16_001_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH02_SC16_001_MARIAM.caption: Sample A has very low conductivity, but Samples B and C both conduct strongly. We still cannot tell which one is baking soda and which one is salt.

CH02_SC16_003_SAEED.speaker: SAEED
CH02_SC16_003_SAEED.caption: So we need another independent property.

CH02_SC17_002_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH02_SC17_002_NARRATOR.caption: A P H value near seven is neutral under these simulation conditions. A value above seven indicates basic behavior.

CH02_SC17_003_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC17_003_SYSTEM.caption: Sample A P H: seven point zero. Sample B P H: eight point three. Sample C P H: seven point zero.

CH02_SC17_004_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH02_SC17_004_MARIAM.caption: Sample B is mildly basic. Samples A and C are neutral in this simulation.

CH02_SC18_001_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC18_001_HAMAD.caption: We will now perform a controlled virtual reaction using a dilute acid and separate portions of each prepared sample.

CH02_SC18_004_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC18_004_SYSTEM.caption: Sample A: no visible gas formation.

CH02_SC18_005_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC18_005_SYSTEM.caption: Sample B: carbon dioxide gas detected.

CH02_SC18_007_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC18_007_HAMAD.caption: That reaction is consistent with the presence of hydrogen carbonate ions.

CH02_SC18_008_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC18_008_SYSTEM.caption: Sample C: no visible gas formation.

CH02_SC19_003_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC19_003_HAMAD.caption: Use the combined evidence to identify sucrose, sodium hydrogen carbonate, and sodium chloride.

CH02_SC19_A_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC19_A_SYSTEM.caption: Sample A: sucrose, or table sugar.

CH02_SC19_B_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC19_B_SYSTEM.caption: Sample B: sodium hydrogen carbonate, or baking soda.

CH02_SC19_C_SYSTEM.speaker: SYSTEM
CH02_SC19_C_SYSTEM.caption: Sample C: sodium chloride, or table salt.

CH02_SC19_WRONG_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH02_SC19_WRONG_HAMAD.caption: That assignment does not match all three observations. Review the conductivity, P H, and virtual acid-test results together. A defensible identification must explain every relevant observation, not only one of them.

CH03_SC20_001_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH03_SC20_001_MARIAM.caption: We know which sample is sugar, and we know which sample is baking soda. Can we return them to the preparation station?

CH03_SC20_003_FATIMA.speaker: FATIMA
CH03_SC20_003_FATIMA.caption: Before I authorize anything, I need a clear safety recommendation.

CH03_SC22_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH03_SC22_001_NARRATOR.caption: The evidence is complete. The responsibility now belongs to the investigator.

CH03_SC22_002_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH03_SC22_002_HAMAD.caption: Choose the action you can defend scientifically and professionally. Your decision must account for both the laboratory evidence and the limits of that evidence.

CH04_END_A_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH04_END_A_001_NARRATOR.caption: You choose to document the scientific findings, isolate all three unidentified containers, and replace them with new, sealed ingredients from a traceable food source.

CH04_END_A_004_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH04_END_A_004_MARIAM.caption: The replacement sugar and baking soda are sealed, identified, and verified. We can continue safely.

CH04_END_A_005_SAEED.speaker: SAEED
CH04_END_A_005_SAEED.caption: We lost a little time, but we did not risk serving an unverified ingredient.

CH04_END_A_007_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH04_END_A_007_HAMAD.caption: Strong decision. You used the evidence correctly and respected its limits. Scientific confidence does not mean claiming more than the investigation can prove.

CH04_END_B_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH04_END_B_001_NARRATOR.caption: You choose to use the powder with the lowest conductivity because the data suggest that it is sucrose.

CH04_END_B_004_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH04_END_B_004_HAMAD.caption: Low conductivity helps distinguish sucrose from the two ionic candidates in this investigation. It does not verify that the material is suitable for consumption.

CH04_END_B_005_FATIMA.speaker: FATIMA
CH04_END_B_005_FATIMA.caption: Preparation must stop. Any batch connected to an unverified ingredient must be discarded.

CH04_END_B_007_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH04_END_B_007_NARRATOR.caption: The affected preparation is discarded, and the final round is delayed while verified ingredients are obtained.

CH04_END_C_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH04_END_C_001_NARRATOR.caption: You suggest tasting the powders as a quick way to confirm their identities.

CH04_END_C_002_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH04_END_C_002_HAMAD.caption: Stop. Do not open the container.

CH04_END_C_004_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH04_END_C_004_HAMAD.caption: Tasting is not an acceptable test for an unidentified material. It creates direct exposure while providing weak and subjective evidence.

CH04_END_C_007_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH04_END_C_007_NARRATOR.caption: The unsafe action is prevented before any container is opened. No one is exposed, but additional preparation time is lost while the team returns to the correct safety procedure.

CH04_END_D_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH04_END_D_001_NARRATOR.caption: You choose to identify the powders according to which one appears whitest.

CH04_END_D_002_MARIAM.speaker: MARIAM
CH04_END_D_002_MARIAM.caption: Under the inspection light, they still look almost identical.

CH04_END_D_004_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH04_END_D_004_HAMAD.caption: Whiteness is not a unique chemical property. Lighting, particle size, surface reflection, and the container itself can all affect visual appearance.

CH04_END_D_006_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH04_END_D_006_NARRATOR.caption: The team must restart using ingredients with clear labels and traceable sources. The attempt to save time through appearance creates further delay.

CH05_Q01_CORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q01_CORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Correct. Sodium loses one electron. It then has eleven protons and ten electrons, producing a net charge of positive one.

CH05_Q01_INCORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q01_INCORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Not quite. A positive ion forms when an atom has fewer electrons than protons. Sodium becomes positive by losing one electron.

CH05_Q01_QUESTION_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_Q01_QUESTION_NARRATOR.caption: How does a neutral sodium atom become a positively charged sodium ion?

CH05_Q02_CORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q02_CORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Correct. Chlorine gains one electron. It then has seventeen protons and eighteen electrons, producing a net charge of negative one.

CH05_Q02_INCORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q02_INCORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Review the relationship between protons and electrons. Chlorine becomes negatively charged by gaining one electron.

CH05_Q02_QUESTION_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_Q02_QUESTION_NARRATOR.caption: How does a neutral chlorine atom become a negatively charged chloride ion?

CH05_Q03_CORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q03_CORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Correct. Sodium chloride separates into mobile sodium and chloride ions in water. Those charged particles carry electrical current through the solution.

CH05_Q03_INCORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q03_INCORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Conductivity is not caused simply by the presence of water or by the white color of the solid. It depends on mobile charged particles in the solution.

CH05_Q03_QUESTION_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_Q03_QUESTION_NARRATOR.caption: Why does an aqueous sodium chloride solution conduct electricity?

CH05_Q04_CORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q04_CORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Correct. Sucrose dissolves mainly as neutral molecules and does not produce the same concentration of mobile ions as sodium chloride.

CH05_Q04_INCORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q04_INCORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Dissolving and ionizing are not the same process. Sucrose can dissolve while remaining mainly as neutral molecules.

CH05_Q04_QUESTION_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_Q04_QUESTION_NARRATOR.caption: Why does a sucrose solution conduct electricity much less effectively than a sodium chloride solution under the simulation conditions?

CH05_Q05_CORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q05_CORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Correct. A single test may be shared by different substances. Independent evidence increases confidence and helps distinguish between candidates with similar properties.

CH05_Q05_INCORRECT_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_Q05_INCORRECT_HAMAD.caption: Conductivity showed that Samples B and C both produced mobile ions, but it did not uniquely distinguish them. Additional evidence was required.

CH05_Q05_QUESTION_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_Q05_QUESTION_NARRATOR.caption: Why was it necessary to combine conductivity, P H, and controlled reaction evidence?

CH05_QUIZ_INTRO_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_QUIZ_INTRO_NARRATOR.caption: Answer five questions about ions, conductivity, molecular substances, and evidence-based identification. You need at least four correct answers out of five to earn the Ionic Evidence Investigator achievement.

CH05_REFLECTION_001_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_REFLECTION_001_NARRATOR.caption: You have seen the consequences of your decision. Now reflect on the reasoning that produced it.

CH05_REFLECTION_002_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_REFLECTION_002_HAMAD.caption: Explain what you learned from the outcome. Refer to at least one piece of scientific evidence from the investigation. State what you would keep or change if you faced a similar decision again.

CH05_SC27_001_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_SC27_001_HAMAD.caption: Today, you investigated the invisible chemistry behind familiar everyday materials.

CH05_SC27_002_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_SC27_002_HAMAD.caption: You observed that substances can look alike and still behave differently. You used conductivity to investigate the presence of mobile charged particles. You used P H and controlled reaction behavior to distinguish between two ionic substances. And you combined independent observations instead of relying on one result.

CH05_SC27_006_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_SC27_006_NARRATOR.caption: The investigation is complete. One final assessment remains.

CH05_SC28_PASS_1_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_SC28_PASS_1_NARRATOR.caption: Assessment complete. You answered at least four of the five questions correctly.

CH05_SC28_PASS_2_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_SC28_PASS_2_HAMAD.caption: Well done. You have earned the Ionic Evidence Investigator achievement.

CH05_SC28_RETRY_1_NARRATOR.speaker: NARRATOR
CH05_SC28_RETRY_1_NARRATOR.caption: Assessment complete. Your result has been recorded, but the achievement requires at least four correct answers out of five.

CH05_SC28_RETRY_2_HAMAD.speaker: HAMAD
CH05_SC28_RETRY_2_HAMAD.caption: Review the feedback carefully. Focus on electron transfer, mobile ions, the difference between dissolving and ionizing, and the value of combining independent tests.
